proposal: Consider the hidden subgroup problem over S_n whose hidden subgroups are indexed by the (n-1)!! perfect matchings of n points, so information-theoretically about log2((n-1)!!) coset-state copies are needed; call this number k. Block-encode the Gram (metric) operator of the k-copy ensemble as a tensor product of linear-combination-of-unitaries encodings of single copies and of pairs of copies, each rescaled by its rank to have bounded normalization, and conclude that the full metric is available with polynomial normalization.
killer: LCU normalization factors multiply across tensor factors. On almost all of the natural input mass each singleton or pair factor costs at least sqrt(2) per copy, so every such local partition has total normalization at least 2^(k/2), which is superpolynomial (2^(Theta(n log n))) at this k.
lesson: Normalizations of tensor-product block encodings compound multiplicatively, so any per-factor constant above one becomes exponential in the number of factors; threshold-scale copy counts need a global transform rather than local blocks.

proposal: Regev's reduction turns a classical subset-sum solver modulo N = 2^n that succeeds on an inverse-polynomial fraction of random instances into a quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem. As that solver, multiply the instance (a_1, ..., a_m; t) by each of polynomially many random odd residues u mod 2^n, run LLL on the standard lattice embedding of every rescaled copy, and output any valid solution; on small sizes this rescues many instances that LLL misses on the original presentation.
killer: Multiplying by a unit mod 2^n leaves the problem unchanged: the relation lattice {y : sum a_i y_i = 0 mod 2^n} and the solution set of (u a, u t) coincide with the original ones, so the method only re-randomizes the basis handed to LLL. Nothing shows that basis re-randomization lifts LLL from a vanishing to an inverse-polynomial success rate on random density-one instances, so finite rescues give no coverage guarantee of the kind the reduction requires.
lesson: A rescaling that maps an instance to an equivalent one cannot change its intrinsic hardness; heuristic re-randomizations of a lattice basis need an average-case coverage theorem before they count as a solver.

proposal: In subset-sum instances modulo 2^m that arise from the dihedral coset problem, the Boolean function giving a high-order carry bit of sum_i a_i x_i in terms of the input bits x has algebraic normal form (ANF) of degree growing linearly in m. First apply a dense random invertible affine change of variables x -> Ax + b over GF(2), hoping that in the new coordinates the carry function has bounded degree and can be reconstructed from polynomially many monomials.
killer: Algebraic degree over GF(2) is invariant under invertible affine substitutions: composing with an affine map cannot raise the degree, and composing back with its inverse shows it cannot lower it either. The carry function therefore keeps degree Theta(m), with exponentially many monomials, in every GL(m,2) coordinate system.
lesson: Degree-based obstructions for Boolean functions survive every linear or affine re-coordinatization, so lowering degree requires auxiliary variables or a nonlinear reformulation.

proposal: In Kuperberg-style sieving for the dihedral coset problem over Z_N with N = 2^n, each register has the form (|0> + exp(2 pi i k s / N)|1>)/sqrt(2) with a known label k and hidden shift s. Once the sieve outputs a register whose label is k = N/2, measure it in the Hadamard basis and read off s, which recovers the hidden reflection.
killer: With k = N/2 the relative phase is (-1)^s, so the Hadamard measurement returns only the parity s mod 2. The remaining n-1 bits require rerunning the sieve on a reduced problem for each bit (or another recursion), and the correctness and cost of that full recursive decoder are a separate obligation.
lesson: A sieve endpoint at the highest 2-adic valuation yields a single parity bit, so count decoded bits and analyze the whole bit-by-bit recursion before claiming recovery of the hidden shift.

proposal: Let J_1, ..., J_w be isometric embeddings of child spaces into a parent space whose frame operator S = sum_e J_e J_e^* has spectrum in a fixed constant window on its support, and suppose each pairwise overlap J_f^* J_e is available as a normalization-one block encoding. Plan: produce the whitened blocks J_f^* W U W J_e, where W = S^(-1/2) and U is a fixed parent unitary, with O(1) overlap queries by applying quantum singular value transformation to obtain polar parts of the individual pair overlaps and then combining them.
killer: S^(-1/2) depends on all w children at once and cannot be read off from any pair: pairwise polar decompositions see only two-element Gram data and discard the global positive metric. Assembling the w overlaps coherently with uniform weights yields only the analysis map divided by sqrt(w) (or the Gram matrix divided by w), whose relevant singular values are Theta(1/sqrt(w)), so extracting its polar part with bounded QSVT polynomials needs degree Omega(sqrt(w)), not O(1).
lesson: Canonical (Lowdin-type) frame whitening is a global functional of the whole frame, so local polar steps cannot replace it and coherent aggregation pays the frame's normalization in polynomial degree.

proposal: In the hidden subgroup problem over S_n with hidden subgroup {e, h} for an unknown transposition h, the multi-copy frame operator on copies of the standard representation rho is built from pair operators K_ij, each the sum over transpositions h of rho(h) tensor rho(h) acting on copies i and j. For two copies the Kronecker (Clebsch-Gordan) decomposition of rho tensor rho diagonalizes the frame, so for three copies use the basis that couples copies 1 and 2 first and then adjoins copy 3, expecting it to diagonalize the three-copy frame as well.
killer: Frames on three copies involve K_12, K_23 and K_13, which do not commute: an explicit matrix entry of [K_12, K_23] equals n for every n >= 3. A basis adapted to the (12)3 coupling diagonalizes K_12 alone, so diagonalizing the frame needs the Racah (6j, associator) transformation between the (12)3 and 1(23) couplings together with decoding of multiplicity spaces.
lesson: Before extending a pairwise coupling basis to three or more tensor factors, check whether the pair operators on overlapping factors commute; if they do not, recoupling (6j) transformations are unavoidable.

proposal: In the shifted Legendre symbol problem one is given oracle access to x -> ((x + s)/p) for a prime p and must find the hidden shift s. By the Weil bound two distinct shifts agree on only about half of the inputs, so O(log p) random queries determine s uniquely; therefore a classical algorithm can recover s in time polynomial in log p.
killer: Query complexity is not time complexity: identifying which shift is consistent with the O(log p) answers is a search over p candidates (equivalently, solving polynomial equations of degree about p/2), and no classical algorithm running in poly(log p) time is known. The problem underlies the Legendre pseudorandom function assumption, the best classical attacks take time exponential in log p, and only the quantum algorithm of van Dam, Hallgren and Ip solves it efficiently.
lesson: Information-theoretic identifiability from few samples says nothing about efficient decoding; separate sample complexity from the cost of inverting the measurement map.

proposal: To pair dihedral coset registers whose labels a_1, ..., a_m are residues mod 2^n, search for a sparse relation, a 0/1 vector x of Hamming weight at most r with sum a_i x_i equal to a prescribed residue, by streaming through all supports of weight up to r in increasing order and testing each with reversible XOR arithmetic in polynomial workspace. Because the workspace and the description of the search are both polynomial, the pairing finder runs in polynomial time.
killer: Small memory does not bound running time. A relation typically exists only once the number of candidate supports D = sum_{w <= r} C(m, w) reaches about 2^n, and the stream tests every one of them, so the cost is at least on the order of 2^n predicate evaluations (12 * 2^n for this evaluator) before any arithmetic; Grover-style search would cut this only to about 2^(n/2).
lesson: Exhaustive enumeration with polynomial space is still exponential time whenever the solution density forces the candidate count past the modulus; a speedup needs a structured solver, not a streamed one.

proposal: Dinh, Moore and Russell proved that, in the hidden-subgroup formulation of linear code equivalence relevant to McEliece, measurements on a single coset state yield negligible information about the hidden subgroup. Apply their theorem to rule out single-coset-state quantum Fourier sampling for equivalence of self-dual codes, for instance binary self-dual codes of length 24.
killer: Their result is a sufficient condition whose hypotheses include q^(k^2) <= n^(0.2n), which controls the GL_k(F_q) factor of the group. Self-duality forces k = n/2, so q^(k^2) = q^(n^2/4) overwhelms n^(0.2n) at every interesting length (for q = 2, n = 24 it is 2^144 against about 2^22); the theorem does not apply and the question stays open rather than settled either way.
lesson: Check every hypothesis of a sufficient no-go theorem (dimension, automorphism size, minimal degree) against the instance family; a failed hypothesis leaves proof debt, not a closed route.

proposal: In a hierarchical measurement that merges two child subsystems at a time, the final merge is governed by two positive operators A and B on a D-dimensional space whose spectra stay inside fixed intervals, independent of D, bounded away from 0 and 1. Conjecture that this bounded arity and good conditioning force the algebra generated by A and B to have dimension polynomial in log D, so the merge can be compiled by working inside that small algebra.
killer: Conditioning places no constraint on the generated algebra. If A has D distinct eigenvalues, polynomials in A give its rank-one eigenprojectors P_i, and if every off-diagonal block P_i B P_j is nonzero these products are nonzero multiples of matrix units, so the pair generates all of M_D(C), of dimension D^2; both spectra can be confined to any prescribed window, e.g. A = cI plus a small diagonal and B = cI plus a small generic perturbation.
lesson: The dimension of the algebra that a few well-conditioned operators generate is generically full, so it is neither a compilation route nor a circuit lower bound; look for succinct block encodings instead.

proposal: The quantum-walk algorithm for random subset-sum running in time about 2^(0.2182n), due to Bonnetain, Bricout, Schrottenloher and Shen, can be set aside as a baseline in subset-sum-based approaches to the dihedral coset problem: like other walks over lists stored in quantum memory, its data-structure updates depend on the order of past insertions and leave path-dependent garbage that destroys the interference the walk needs.
killer: That algorithm was designed to avoid exactly this: it stores its lists in a history-independent quantum data structure, so each set has a unique memory representation regardless of insertion order, and its update error is bounded independently of the data. A generic garbage counterexample for walks with order-dependent memory layout therefore does not transfer to it.
lesson: Before invoking a known obstruction against a published algorithm, check whether the source already repairs the specific mechanism the obstruction exploits.

proposal: For a random density-one subset-sum instance with labels a_1, ..., a_m mod 2^n, the uniform superposition over the solution fiber {x in {0,1}^m : sum a_i x_i = t mod 2^n} requires exponential matrix-product-state bond dimension, even approximately, for any fixed ordering of the coordinates, except on a negligible fraction of label choices. Get around this by preparing a polynomial-size dictionary of coordinate orderings in advance and, on each instance, using whichever ordering yields a small bond dimension.
killer: The dictionary is chosen before the labels are drawn, so a union bound over its polynomially many orderings shows that with high probability every listed ordering still needs exponential bond dimension. Allowing polynomial approximation slack does not lower the exponential rank either.
lesson: A fixed polynomial family of choices made independently of a random instance cannot beat an obstruction that holds for each choice with overwhelming probability; adaptivity to the instance is required.

proposal: Small-size computations of the algebraic normal form (ANF) of the carry bits of sum_i a_i x_i for random density-one subset-sum instances suggest these bits have modest degree. Encode an instance as the resulting system of low-degree polynomial equations over GF(2) in the bits of x and solve it by linearization, giving a polynomial-time algebraic subset-sum solver.
killer: Even granting low degree d, an instance gives only about n equations (one per output bit) in m of about n unknowns, while linearization needs as many independent equations as monomials, about m^d; solving a handful of low-degree GF(2) equations is the NP-hard MQ problem and believed hard on random instances. In addition, the ANF tables come from exponential-size truth tables, and small-size degree trends are not a uniform bound (high carry bits have degree linear in m).
lesson: A compact polynomial-system formulation of a hard problem is not a solver; account for the equation-to-monomial ratio and the cost of computing the system itself.

proposal: In the dihedral coset problem over Z_N with N = 2^n, each register carries a uniformly random known label k, and combining two registers with labels k and k' yields a register with label k - k' or k + k'. Rather than running Kuperberg's multi-stage sieve, collect registers until two labels sum or differ by exactly N/2, combine them to reach label N/2 in a single step, and claim a subexponential improvement over sieving.
killer: For uniform labels a given pair hits the prescribed difference or sum with probability about 2/N, so among M registers one expects about M^2/N hits and M must be about sqrt(N) = 2^(n/2). This is an exponential birthday search, far worse than Kuperberg's 2^(O(sqrt(n))), and finite fits indeed scale linearly in n with slope near 1/2.
lesson: Hitting one prescribed label from random labels is a birthday problem costing about sqrt(N); subexponential sieves must reduce labels gradually through many cheap collisions.

proposal: Let B be the average of the projectors onto the coset states of a hidden subgroup problem over S_n, given as a normalization-one block encoding; its informative eigenvalues sit at scale about 1/n!. Implement the spectral trimming needed for a constant-success measurement, keeping eigenvalues above a cutoff of order 1/n! and suppressing those below, by applying a generic bounded polynomial to B with quantum singular value transformation at polynomial degree.
killer: A bounded polynomial that moves from near 0 to a constant across a window of width Theta(1/n!) must have a derivative of order n! there, and Bernstein's (or Markov's) inequality then forces degree Omega(n!) for an eigenvalue transform, or Omega(sqrt(n!)) for a singular-value transform; both are superpolynomial.
lesson: QSVT degree scales inversely with the spectral gap being resolved, so block encodings whose relevant eigenvalues are factorially small need rescaling or an exact representation-theoretic classifier, not generic polynomials.

proposal: For lambda drawn from the Plancherel measure on S_n, consider the averaged measure on conjugacy classes nu(C) = E_lambda[|C| chi_lambda(C)^2 / n!], which is a probability distribution by orthogonality of characters. Small-n computations show its nonidentity mass is dominated by classes moving few points, so conjecture that the classes whose set of moved points has size no larger than n^delta, for some delta < 1, keep constant total mass as n grows, and build an asymptotic mechanism on these near-identity classes.
killer: By column orthogonality the squared character values at a fixed class C sum to n!/|C| over all lambda, so nu(C) never exceeds the largest single Plancherel probability, which is exp(-Theta(sqrt(n))). Only exp(O(n^(delta/2))) conjugacy classes have support of size <= n^delta (at most the sum of partition numbers p(j) for j up to n^delta), so their combined mass is o(1) for every delta < 1.
lesson: Mass concentrated on low-support classes at small n can evaporate asymptotically; compare the number of classes in a family against the maximal Plancherel atom before extrapolating.

proposal: To handle typical irreducible representations of S_n, those drawn from the Plancherel measure (lambda with probability d_lambda^2/n!), precompute offline an exact partition-specific certificate, for instance a recoupling table, for each partition in a polynomial-size catalog of the most likely shapes, and use it whenever the sampled lambda lies in the catalog. Since Plancherel-random partitions concentrate around the Vershik-Kerov-Logan-Shepp limit shape, such a catalog should cover a constant fraction of the measure.
killer: Concentration on the limit shape is only macroscopic: the largest single Plancherel probability is exp(-Theta(sqrt(n))), so a catalog covering constant mass needs exp(Omega(sqrt(n))) partitions, which is superpolynomial.
lesson: When inputs follow a measure whose atoms are all exponentially small, no polynomial lookup table can cover constant mass; one needs a uniform rule parameterized by the input description.

proposal: Each dihedral coset register (|0> + exp(2 pi i k s / N)|1>)/sqrt(2) with a known uniformly random label k, measured in the Hadamard basis, gives a noisy sample of the character k -> exp(2 pi i k s / N). Recover s from such samples with the significant Fourier transform of Akavia, Goldwasser and Safra, or with a chosen-multiplier hidden number problem algorithm, both of which find a hidden frequency in poly(log N) time.
killer: Those algorithms rely on query access: they choose correlated evaluation points (shifts, multiples, intervals) and may repeat them. The dihedral coset problem supplies only independent uniformly random labels, each usable once, with no evaluator, no repeats, no interval conditioning and no chosen multipliers, and in this random-sample model the best known algorithms (Kuperberg-type sieves) remain superpolynomial.
lesson: Classify a Fourier-learning algorithm by its access model (chosen queries versus random samples) before importing its runtime.

proposal: Kuperberg's sieve for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem on Z_N cancels about sqrt(log N) bits of the labels per stage. Numerically search over the constant c in schedules that cancel c*sqrt(log N) bits per stage, choose the c that minimizes simulated cost, and present the tuned schedule as a new asymptotically faster algorithm.
killer: Every schedule of this form still runs in 2^(Theta(sqrt(log N))) time, the same class as Kuperberg's original algorithm and his later collimation sieve, so tuning c changes at most the constant in the exponent. A schedule picked by finite simulation also comes with no proved recurrence, so even that constant-level gain is not established.
lesson: Re-tuning constants inside a known recurrence strengthens the baseline; evidence of asymptotic progress requires a new recurrence with a proof.

proposal: For random modular subset-sum at density one (m residues a_i uniform modulo M of size about 2^m, and target t = sum a_i x_i for a planted 0/1 vector x), embed the instance in the standard Lagarias-Odlyzko style lattice so that x appears as a short vector, and argue that it is the unique shortest vector, or isolated among the shortest, so that a unique-SVP or bounded-distance-decoding oracle extracts it.
killer: At density one the relation lattice is crowded: signed vectors y in {-1,0,1}^m with m/4 nonzero entries number C(m, m/4) 2^(m/4), about 2^(1.06m), and each satisfies sum a_i y_i = 0 mod M with probability about 2^(-m), so roughly 2^(0.06m) such relations exist (the count concentrates), each no longer than the planted witness. There is no uniqueness gap, consistent with lattice attacks working only below density about 0.94.
lesson: Before relying on uniqueness of a planted short vector, count competing short lattice vectors with first- and second-moment arguments at the target density.

proposal: Given m = O(log N) measured dihedral coset samples (k_i, b_i) with uniformly random labels k_i in Z_N, the likelihood of a candidate shift s is a product of factors cos^2 or sin^2 of pi k_i s / N, maximized at the hidden shift. Find the maximizer by branch-and-bound over intervals of s, pruning each interval with separable Lipschitz upper bounds on the individual factors, and expect poly(log N) running time.
killer: Uniform labels are typically of size Theta(N), so each factor oscillates with period about N/k_i = O(1) in s; over any interval much longer than a constant the factor's bound saturates at 1, and pruning becomes effective only on intervals of constant length. Branch-and-bound therefore explores on the order of N candidates, exponential in log N.
lesson: Interval or Lipschitz bounds are useless on likelihoods built from high-frequency random characters; localization needs a global, nonseparable certificate or algebraic structure.
